newsitem.title: USA: Russia tempts U.S. bond investors despite politics.
newsitem.headline: Russia tempts U.S. bond investors despite politics.

text.p: The perils of Russian politics failed to rattle U.S. investors, who shrugged off a rumor, later denied, that President Boris Yeltsin had died.
U.S. portfolio managers said Wednesday that Russian bonds, despite spectacular returns higher than 100 percent this year, have potential for even further gains.
"Russia will continue to be, if not the best, than one of the best-performing assets in the emerging debt market," said Peter Lannigan, portfolio manager of the Phoenix Emerging Market Bond Fund.

Phoenix led other funds in a Lipper Analytical Services emerging debt poll last month based on its strong presence in Russia, and Lannigan said he would maintain an 18 percent allocation there. "The market will continue to do well and Russia will continue to do better," Lannigan said.

Russian bond prices, which are up 12 percent in October, came off their highs Wednesday morning when rumors of Yeltsin's demise emerged. But prices held on to slight gains as the Russian government shot down the talk.
On Wednesday, Russian Vneshekonombank dollar paper RUVNUSLNS=RR closed 1/4 higher to a bid price of 79-1/2, and mark vnesh rose 5/6 to 84-1/4, even as the overall emerging debt market slipped.

Analysts said that, as Russian stripped yields traded more than 7.5 percent higher than Treasuries-against-Mexican spreads of about 460 basis points, investors were being well compensated for the risk.

"Russian debt prices are tight relative to where they were, but relative to everything else in the market they still look cheap," said Steve Merrell, senior portfolio manager at American Express Financial Services.
Analysts said the country's recent credit rating, improved inflation outlook, export earning potential and restructured bank debt provided stability to its macroeconomic picture.
Earlier this week, Standard and Poor's assigned Russia a BB-minus long-term foreign debt rating, and Moody's Investors Service issued a Ba2 sovereign ceiling.

While Russia's economic fundamentals appeared healthy, the financial markets expected uncertainty in the country's political scene, evidenced by the wide spreads of Russian bond compared with comparably rated credits.

"They are discounting quite a lot of political problems in Russia," Luis R. Luis, director of emerging market analysis at Scudder Stevens & Clark, a Boston-based mutual fund with $2.0 billion dedicated to emerging market debt.
"During this time the markets are likely to show some periods of high volaitlity," Luis said. "One has to ride that out. ...In terms of relative value it certainly has value."
Analysts agreed that Russian debt prices would probably drop if Yeltsin were to die soon, but several saw the uncertainty as a buying opportunity.
"There's enough yield in those entities that people can feel feel comfortable about the numbers and still get more return," said an emerging market analyst at a major U.S. mutual fund.
